title: Does Power Corrupt?
text:
In 1972 the psychologist David Kipnis reported a simple experiment on what power does to the way managers see the people below them. Students were asked to play the role of a manager supervising a small team of workers who were supposedly in another room, doing a task and sending in their results.

Half of the managers were given real levers of power. They could raise or cut the workers' pay, give or deny bonuses, threaten to fire them, transfer them, or give them extra instruction. The other half had no such powers and could only try to persuade.

Managers with power used it, and the more they used it, the more their view of the workers changed. Compared with managers without power, they tended to rate the workers as less capable and less worthy, credited the work more to their own control than to the workers' motivation, wanted more distance from them socially, and were less interested in meeting them. Kipnis concluded that holding the means to control people tends to make leaders value those people less.
lesson: When you can command, it is tempting to credit yourself for others' work. Keep asking what your people contribute on their own, and stay close to them.
source: Kipnis, D. (1972). Does power corrupt? Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 24(1), 33-41.
caveat: It was a role-play with students, not real managers, so it shows a tendency rather than how every leader behaves.
